html:
From one of my Zhihu answers

The question: I’m about to start my last year of high school, and I’m a headphone enthusiast. When I look this major up online there’s very little information, and it doesn’t seem to be a popular choice.
I’d sincerely like to ask about the courses and the job prospects.
Thanks
P.S. I have Grade 10 in electronic keyboard and know my music theory
P.P.S. Does this major require music theory too?
P.P.P.S. My physics grades are great right now, but I’m not into math

To the young man or woman who asked this question, now about to graduate from university, my warmest regards: have you started your final-year project yet? And did anyone stop you back then?

I know exactly how you feel. When I first came across acoustics, I had no idea what it was actually about; all I knew was that reducing noise seemed to be its only goal. I stumbled into the field because the supervisor I picked happened to work in acoustics. Just as when I chose my university major, I drifted into a field quite passively. Fortunately, over the years, the more I learned about the discipline, the more I came to love it. Perhaps it’s my compensation for four miserable years in the wrong undergraduate major.

Psychoacoustics

My master’s project was related to psychoacoustics, my first real contact with acoustics. At the time I read a lot of Chinese papers, mainly from Jilin University, Southwest Jiaotong University and Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Back then not much acoustics, and especially psychoacoustics, was being done in China, so there was little literature to draw on. Our group bought an artificial head, and from the software manual I learned the algorithms behind the various psychoacoustic parameters. But I felt the manual didn’t go into enough detail, so I found Professor Zwicker’s Psychoacoustics and chewed my way through it for a while. It was the first specialist acoustics book I ever read, and there was a lot in it I didn’t understand. When I graduated, I looked around and saw nobody hiring in acoustics. As I recall, only Goertek explicitly asked for people with an acoustics background. Because of my master’s topic, the PhD positions I applied for were all related to acoustics. And so, without quite knowing what I was doing, I ended up in acoustics.

Careers:

Carmakers. One look at HEAD acoustics’ list of OEM customers tells you how important psychoacoustics is to the auto industry. Once noise levels have been brought down far enough, people realize that sound has “quality,” so besides sound pressure level, the main psychoacoustic parameters have become key metrics to monitor. Sound design is another option.

Virtual acoustics

During my PhD I moved into virtual acoustics, modeling moving sound sources. The institute also worked on other areas, such as architectural and medical acoustics, so I gradually got to know those too. As I said in an earlier answer, virtual acoustics covers source modeling, propagation modeling and 3D reproduction, plus the algorithms and hardware needed for real-time auralization. At first I had no idea where to begin, and my boss wasn’t entirely sure how to go about it either. I stumbled along on my own until I eventually settled on extracting the source signals with beamforming.

Careers:

Companies working on the built environment. Arup, for example: its acoustics group in Amsterdam works mainly on virtual acoustics and has its own VR lab. I have seen their demos, auralizations of passing trains and of wind turbines, which focus mainly on 3D reproduction. Another well-known name is Müller-BBM in Germany.

VR and AR companies. Facebook Reality Labs (formerly Oculus), for example, covers the whole spectrum: numerical and geometric modeling of indoor and outdoor sound propagation, 3D reproduction, binaural hearing and HRTFs, real-time algorithms and more. Some of my former colleagues have gone to Huawei’s R&D center in Munich to work on spatial audio, and the big headphone and loudspeaker makers, such as Bose and Sennheiser, are all investing in this area.

Carmakers and the speech industry (beamforming). Beamforming is mainly used for source localization. In voice interaction, Amazon, Google, Apple, Xiaomi and others all use it to locate the person speaking, suppress background noise and make the voice easier to understand.

Numerical acoustics and architectural acoustics

During a one-year postdoc I got into numerical acoustics, a direction I had never worked in before, and picked up some knowledge of acoustic metamaterials. Numerical acoustics is mainly about modeling sound propagation: within rooms, between rooms, outdoors, from outdoors to indoors and back, between the floors of a building, and so on. There is a whole zoo of methods, from the classic BEM and FEM to FVM, PSTD and DG, in both the frequency and the time domain. If there is one area of acoustics I am still not especially fond of, it is probably numerical acoustics. Maybe I’m just not good enough at it, but it has never captured my interest.

Careers:

The larger acoustics departments of the companies mentioned above all have people doing numerical simulation in the early stages of development. Other strong companies in numerical work include Siemens (formerly LMS) and COMSOL. Architectural acoustics means the many institutes and companies working on the built environment, mainly on room acoustic design for auditoriums and on noise reduction in buildings and their surroundings.

The curriculum

Take RWTH Aachen University as an example. Its Institute of Technical Acoustics belongs to the Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Information Technology, so the core courses of that broader field are compulsory. In acoustics itself, the bachelor’s program offers an introduction to acoustics and the basics of noise control; the master’s program offers technical acoustics, psychoacoustics, sound engineering, medical acoustics, virtual acoustics and electroacoustics, along with the accompanying lab courses.

Beyond the core courses, RWTH’s first-year MATLAB Mindstorms course is great fun (mindstorms.rwth-aachen.de). It is a two-week course with Lego: students program Lego robots in MATLAB to reach a set goal, such as a car that steers around obstacles by itself or a robot that plays the guitar. Seeing how much fun these kids have with it every year makes me want to buy a Mindstorms set and play with it myself.

I also highly recommend the edX MOOC Communication Acoustics, a foundational acoustics course run jointly by professors from several of Europe’s top universities.

https://www.edx.org/course/fundamentals-of-communication-acoustics-2

https://www.edx.org/course/applications-in-communication-acoustics-2

Oh, and for learning acoustics, I recommend the ITA-Toolbox, which I have used for years. It is an excellent MATLAB toolbox for acoustics and a powerful tool for acoustic experiments and analysis:

https://git.rwth-aachen.de/ita/toolbox

Acoustics companies in China

The figure below shows some of the companies I have collected. It doesn’t include other big companies, such as tech firms like Huawei, Xiaomi, Tencent and ByteDance, or the major carmakers, such as SAIC, Geely, BAIC, GAC and FAW. The figure also includes some other companies working in acoustics.

A while ago I searched Qichacha, a Chinese company-information database, for the keyword “acoustics,” and the result gave me quite a shock: 16,553 companies. That would have been unthinkable in the year I finished my master’s.

In September I’ll be at the National Acoustics Conference in Shenzhen. I look forward to talking with many like-minded fellow acousticians!

One more thing

I love acoustics because it spans so many fields: through acoustics you get a window onto all sorts of industries. Another thing that sets acoustics apart is that, where most disciplines stop at what you can see, it adds what you can hear. Especially in virtual acoustics: besides looking at curves and numbers on a screen, you can listen to the results of your simulations or experiments, and that has given me a great deal of joy. It is also why my acoustics WeChat account and Zhihu column came into being.
